leaves.title: Understanding a short spoken description
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice listening for both the general idea and specific facts in a short spoken description — a common real-life listening task, like hearing someone describe a place they know.

Read the transcript below as if you were listening to someone describe their school, then answer the questions about it.

"Our school is small, with about 200 students. My class has only eight students, so the teacher knows everyone well. We're in a small building with a kitchen and a yard. Most classes are in the morning, and some students study in the afternoon too."

When you listen (or read a transcript) for the first time, focus on the general picture — is it a big or small school? When you listen again, focus on the exact numbers and details.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to understand a short spoken description and answer both general and detail questions about it.
examples: General question: Is the school big or small?
Detail question: How many students are in the class?
commonMistakes: Don't try to write down every word — focus on the general picture first, then listen again for details.
Don't confuse similar-sounding numbers (thirteen/thirty) — this connects to what you practiced in the number pronunciation lesson.

exercises.title: Answer the questions
exercises.instructions: Based on the description, answer each question.

questions.prompt: How many students are in the whole school?
How many students are in the class?
What does the building have, besides classrooms?

exercises.title: Choose the correct answer
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that matches the description.

questions.prompt: Is the school big or small?
Does the teacher know the students well?

leaves.title: Completing information from a conversation
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice a common real-life listening task: filling in missing information — like a name, address, or job — while following a conversation, similar to taking notes during a phone call or interview.

Read the transcript below as if you were listening to an interview, then complete the missing information.

Officer: What's the person's name?
Witness: His name is Daniel Cole.
Officer: And his job?
Witness: He's an electrician.
Officer: Where does he live?
Witness: On Baker Street, I think — near the old cinema.
Officer: What time did you see him?
Witness: About six o'clock in the evening.

When completing information from a conversation, listen for the answer immediately after the question — the key information is usually a short phrase right after it's asked.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to pick out and note down specific pieces of information as you follow a conversation.
examples: Question: 'What's his job?' Answer (right after): 'He's an electrician.'
commonMistakes: Don't wait too long after a question to note the answer — in real speech, the key information often comes immediately.
Watch for hedging words like 'I think' — they signal the speaker isn't fully certain, which can matter for accuracy.

exercises.title: Complete the information
exercises.instructions: Based on the conversation, complete each piece of information.

exercises.title: Choose the correct answer
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that matches the conversation.

questions.prompt: Where does the witness think Daniel lives?
How certain is the witness about the address?
